sources.name: Types of Primary Elections: Which Primary Can You Vote In? - FindLaw
How States Differentiate Presidential Primaries From State Primaries - NCSL
Types of Primary Systems, Explained - Unite America

_: As of 2022, California is attempting a Top-Two system, where all registered voters receive one ballot regardless of party affiliation, and the top two move on to the general election.
State does not have party registration.
Florida voters must declare a party in advance to vote in that party's primary.
Voters in New York must be a member of a party to participate in the primary.
Pennsylvania voters must be registered with a party to participate in the primary.

Voters must declare a party at the polling place and can only receive that party’s primary ballot, and those who refuse to state a party cannot vote in the primary. They may also participate in a local party primary if applicable, but cannot vote in more than one statewide par…
Voters may request a party’s primary ballot by declaring support for that party, but eligibility can be challenged based on the voter’s recent primary voting history and party affiliation record.
No partisan registration, and voters are bound to their party if there is a runoff
Unaffiliated voters may choose and vote in one party’s primary by stating their preference at the polling place.
Michigan voters do not declare affiliation but must choose a party's ballot to vote on.
Voters must be a member of a party to participate in the primary.
Virginia voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.

Washington uses a top-two primary system, where all candidates appear on the same primary ballot regardless of party, and the two candidates receiving the most votes advance to the general election, regardless of party preference.
While party members may only vote on that ballot, unaffiliated voters may choose which ballot to vote on.
Voters may participate in a party’s primary only if they are affiliated with that party or formally declare allegiance and intent to affiliate with it at the time of voting.
Massachusetts is a semi-closed primary, where unenrolled voters may choose a party’s primary ballot and registered party members vote only in their own party’s primary.

A voter may participate in a party’s primary only if they previously voted for, or intend to vote for, that party’s nominees in general elections, meaning access is tied to demonstrated party support rather than free choice at the primary.
Missouri voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.
A political party may choose whether to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in its primary election, meaning access for non-party voters depends on party rules rather than being uniformly open.
Unaffiliated voters in Colorado may vote in either party’s primary without registering with that party, but they must choose only one party ballot.
Wisconsin voters do not have to declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote. This choice does not change their affiliation.
No partisan registration, voters may select one primary to vote in
South Carolina voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.
All voters must choose one party's ballot to vote on, but they are not tied to that party. But voters who do not participate in either primary will only be given the amendments/referendum ballot.
Kentucky party-affiliated voters can only vote in that party's primary.

Louisiana uses an all-comers (open) primary system, where all voters can vote for any candidate in the primary regardless of party affiliation, and the top candidates may advance or win depending on majority rules.

A political party may choose whether to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in its primary election, and may also limit which candidates those voters can select, meaning access for non-affiliated voters depends on party rules.

A political party may choose to allow independent voters to participate in its primary election, meaning unaffiliated voter access depends on party permission rather than being automatically available.

Only voters enrolled in a party may vote in that party’s primary, while unaffiliated voters may participate only if permitted by party rules and must choose a single party’s primary when multiple are held.
Utah state law gives parties discretion to determine participation rules. The Democratic Party operates an open primary. ((Open for Democratic Party)

Voters declare a political affiliation at the polling place, and while party members are restricted to their own party’s primary, certain voters—such as those affiliated with minor parties—may receive a nonpartisan ballot instead of a partisan one.
Any registered voter may declare or change party affiliation at the polls on election day and then vote in that party’s primary, with the change recorded in official registration records.
Arkansas state law gives parties discretion to determine participation rules. Both the Democratic and Republican parties operate an open primary.
Kansas state law gives parties discretion to determine participation rules. The Democratic Party operates an open primary. (Open (Democratic Party)
Mississippi voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.

A voter who is not affiliated with a party may choose one major party’s ballot at the primary election without changing their registration, allowing unaffiliated voters to participate in a party primary by selecting a ballot.
Idaho state law gives parties discretion to determine participation rules. The Democratic Party operates an open primary. (Open for Democratic Party)

Registered voters receive ballots based on party affiliation, where party-affiliated voters get their party’s primary ballot and unaffiliated voters receive only nonpartisan ballots unless specific exceptions apply.
Unaffiliated voters may participate in a party primary only if the political party allows it, while otherwise remaining limited to nonpartisan contests and public questions.
Voters may receive ballots for all parties without declaring a party preference, but they may cast votes for candidates of only one party (or the nonpartisan ballot) in the primary election.
Unaffiliated voters may choose a party’s primary ballot on election day and register with that party for the primary, with the option to return to undeclared status afterward.
Unenrolled voters may participate in a party’s primary without enrolling in that party, but they may vote in only one party’s primary election.
Montana voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.
All unaffiliated voters choose one party's ballot to cast their vote in the primary. This choice is viewed as a party declaration.
Delaware voters must declare a party in advance to vote in that party's primary.

A political party may choose whether to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in its primary election, and may also limit which candidates those voters can select, meaning access for non-affiliated voters depends on party rules.
All voters receive a single primary ballot with party sections, and they may choose candidates from only one party section, with votes for multiple parties resulting in rejection of the ballot.
Voters may vote for one candidate per race without consideration for political affiliation. This includes nonpartisan and undeclared.
Vermont voters do not declare affiliation, but they do have to choose a party's ballot to vote.

An elector must declare or change party affiliation before the primary filing period and only then may vote in that party’s primary, meaning participation is limited to voters who formally affiliate with a party.
